meta.note: Hand-kept evidence cards: each fact is tied to a free-to-read source (open-access paper, institute or company report, trade press quoting an authority). Facts marked snippet-level were seen in a search result only. Updated by hand; the publication and news feed below each card is automatic (data/disease_research.json).

context.fact: Norway: sea-phase salmon mortality was 14.2% in 2025 (54.8 million fish), down from 15.4% in 2024 (57.8 million). It was highest in PO4 at 20.1%.
Norway 2025, cause of death (AquaCloud data, 408 sea sites): injuries/trauma 33.5%, infectious disease 28.1%, unknown 27.4%.
Norway 2025: 2.67 million salmon were discarded at slaughter ('utkast'), 0.5% of harvest weight (7,218 t). Superior grade share was 86.9%.
Chile: overall salmon farm mortality was 9.7% in 2025, down 1.5 points from 2024. Infectious causes made up 25.7% of Atlantic salmon mortality, led by SRS (52.8%) and tenacibaculosis (31.5%).

diseases.name: Sea lice
diseases.agent: Lepeophtheirus salmonis (N. Atlantic), Caligus rogercresseyi (Chile); crustacean ectoparasites
diseases.what: Parasitic copepods graze salmon skin. The main supply hit is the delousing itself (thermal, mechanical, freshwater, chemical), which stresses, injures and kills fish and stops growth.

mortality.fact: Norway: elevated mortality followed 31% of thermal treatments, 25% of mechanical, 21% of hydrogen peroxide, and under 14% of azamethiphos, cypermethrin or deltamethrin treatments. Fish of 2 kg or more were more susceptible.
mortality.source: Overton et al., Reviews in Aquaculture, 2019 (IMR open repository)

mortality.fact: Norway 2025: injuries/trauma, driven mainly by mechanical damage from delousing, were the largest recorded cause of sea-phase salmon deaths at 33.5% (AquaCloud, 408 sites).
mortality.source: Norwegian Veterinary Institute, Fiskehelserapporten 2025 (2026)

mortality.fact: Norway 2025: 653 serious welfare incidents in sea farms (44% of all) were linked to non-medicinal delousing, up from 2024. 1,488 incidents in total, versus 1,385 in 2024.
mortality.source: Norwegian Veterinary Institute, Fiskehelserapporten 2025 (2026)

mortality.fact: Norway: thermal or mechanical delousing significantly raised the risk of pasteurellosis outbreaks (reported in FHR 2025, unquantified).
mortality.source: Norwegian Veterinary Institute, Fiskehelserapporten 2025 (2026)

growth.fact: Norway (2014-2019 data, 2,530 treatments): every delousing method reduced short-term growth (TGC), and non-medicinal methods did significantly more harm than medicinal ones. Example: one non-medicinal treatment of a 150,000-fish cage at 3 kg and 10 °C cost about 31,200 kg of biomass.

cost.fact: Norway: an average lice infestation cost about US$0.46 per kg harvested (about 9% of farm revenue). Total damage was about US$436 million in 2011.
cost.source: Abolofia, Wilen & Asche, Marine Resource Economics, 2017 (UiS repository)

cost.fact: Norway: lice cost farmers at least NOK 5.2 billion in 2018, excluding indirect costs (Nofima estimate).
Chile: Caligus and its treatments raised unit production cost by about US$1.4/kg on average (farm cycles 2009-2015).

quality.fact: Norway 2025: only 24% of fish health staff said external injuries after delousing had improved (29% in 2024), and 53% saw no change. Delousing wounds remain a welfare and quality problem.
Context, all causes: in Norway 2025, 0.5% of harvest weight was discarded and 86.9% graded superior. This is not lice-specific.

trend.fact: Norway 2025: record 3,918 non-medicinal delousing treatment-weeks, up 24% from 3,163 in 2024. Mechanical delousing has been the most used method since 2023, and freshwater plus thermal was the most used combination. PO6 averaged about 12 treatment-weeks per site.
Norway 2025: 35% of medicated-feed users and 33% of medicinal-bath users reported reduced effect, and azamethiphos sensitivity is declining.
Chile: hydrogen peroxide use against Caligus roughly doubled, from 5,150.8 g/t in 2023 to 10,890.3 g/t in 2024 (Sernapesca annual reports).
Chile rules: a farm must treat at 6 adult Caligus per fish, and is classed 'high dissemination' at 3 or more ovigerous females after treatment (since 2014).
trend.source: Bravo et al., Frontiers in Aquaculture, 2025 (introduction)

new_research.fact: Norway 2025: Mattilsynet's welfare thresholds for delousing were applied by 78% of surveyed fish health staff, up from 52% in 2024. Exemption sites in PO3/PO4 averaged 3.8 treatment-weeks versus 6.1 at other sites.
USA 2025 challenge test of three salmon strains: tank effects explained 44-50% of the variance in copepodid attachment, versus only 1-7% for strain. About 65% of lice attached to fins.

2025 transcriptomics: lice loads were higher at 20 °C than at 10 °C in most salmon families, and skin gene responses were much larger at 20 °C (3,288 versus 562 shared DEGs). Warming seas may raise lice pressure.
new_research.source: Ghanei-Motlagh et al., Frontiers in Genetics, 2025

diseases.name: Pancreas disease (PD)
diseases.agent: Salmonid alphavirus (SAV2 and SAV3 in Norway; SAV1 in Scotland/Ireland)
diseases.what: A viral disease that damages the pancreas, heart and muscle. It cuts appetite and growth, causes runts and lengthens the production cycle. Mortality is low to moderate, but some outbreaks are severe.

mortality.fact: Norway field trial in a mixed SAV2/SAV3 outbreak: cumulative mortality was 8.9%, about a quarter of it from PD. Cage-level PD mortality ranged from 1.5% to 41.3%.
mortality.source: Røsæg, Thorarinsson & Aunsmo, J Fish Dis 44:1911, 2021 (OA)

mortality.fact: Norway: SAV3 mortality varies from low to moderate but can be high, and SAV2 is generally lower. Deaths start 2-3 weeks after the first signs.
mortality.source: Norwegian Veterinary Institute, PD disease page

mortality.fact: Ireland: PD mortality was 23% in 2007, when about 90% of marine sites were affected, and fell to 2% in 2012. Scotland: PD caused 94% and 86% of disease losses in 2006 and 2007 (older data).
mortality.source: Fish Farming Expert, 2015

growth.fact: Norway outbreak cage study: normalised harvest weight averaged 5.23 kg against an expected 6.31 kg, about 1.1 kg lower.
growth.source: Røsæg et al., J Fish Dis, 2021

growth.fact: Norway: one PD vaccine (Clynav, Clm6) raised harvest weight by 0.43-0.51 kg and cut mortality by 1.3 points (4.5% versus 5.8%) against control. Another vaccine (PDm6) showed no significant weight gain.
growth.source: Røsæg et al., J Fish Dis, 2021

growth.fact: Norway: chronic pancreatic damage lowers growth, raises FCR, creates runts and lengthens the production cycle (qualitative).

cost.fact: Norway: a 2013 SAV3 outbreak cost on average NOK 55.4 million for a sea site stocked with 1 million smolts (Pettersen et al. 2015, cited).
cost.source: Røsæg et al., J Fish Dis, 2021 (citing Pettersen 2015)

quality.fact: Fish with clinical PD had pale, abnormally firm fillets with more collagen and less protein. SAV-infected fish without PD lesions had normal fillet quality (2012 study).
Norway: heart and skeletal-muscle lesions from PD lead to poor slaughter quality.
Norway field trial: superior grade share was 96-98% across cages after the PD outbreak.
quality.source: Røsæg et al., J Fish Dis, 2021

trend.fact: Norway: 44 new PD cases in 2025 (31 SAV3 in PO3-PO4, 13 SAV2 mainly in PO6), down from 48 in 2024, 58 in 2023, 98 in 2022 and 158 in 2020. All 2025 cases were inside the endemic zone.
Norway: 198 million PD vaccine doses were sold for salmon in 2025 (194 million in 2024). Of 50 fish health staff, 58% rated vaccine protection good, 28% medium, and none poor.

new_research.fact: PD resistance is strongly heritable: h2 = 0.41 (pedigree). Two QTL on ssa03 and ssa07 explain more than 60% of the additive genetic variance, making marker-assisted selection for PD-resistant strains possible.
2025: a controlled field trial compared PD vaccines' effects on growth and mortality during an SAV2 outbreak in Norway. Only the title was seen; the full text could not be fetched.

diseases.name: Infectious salmon anaemia (ISA)
diseases.agent: ISA virus (ISAV, orthomyxovirus); HPR-deleted virulent strains, HPR0 low-virulence variant
diseases.what: A notifiable viral disease that causes severe anaemia. Confirmed sites face culling or forced early harvest, restriction zones and fallowing, so each outbreak removes biomass from the market early.

mortality.fact: Norway, 2017-2022: outbreak mortality ranged from 20% to 90%. There were 93 sites with ISA (86 marine farms), and yearly prevalence was 1-3% of the roughly 800 active farms.
mortality.source: Oliveira et al., SVEPM 2025 conference paper

mortality.fact: Norway: daily mortality in affected pens is typically low (about 0.5-1 per 1,000), a 'smouldering fire', although very high mortality has been reported. Diseased fish must be destroyed or slaughtered quickly.
mortality.source: Norwegian Veterinary Institute, ISA page

growth.fact: Vaccinated fish may survive long enough to be harvested rather than destroyed, which costs less. The vaccine reduces mortality and symptoms but does not prevent infection (Pharmaq CEO, Jul 2025).

cost.fact: Chile: the 2007 ISA crisis roughly halved production over three years, with estimated losses of US$600 million.
Iceland 2022: Ice Fish Farm reported a US$9.5 million biomass write-down from ISA losses (headline only).

trend.fact: Norway: ISA was confirmed at 18 sea sites in 2025 (13 in 2024), with 3 more suspected. Seven of the 18 had vaccinated fish, and HPR0 was detected at 78 sites.

Norway, Jan-Jun 2026: 5 confirmed ISA outbreaks (2 in PO6, 2 in PO7, 1 in PO12) plus 2 suspected, versus 11 confirmed in Jan-Jun 2025. The 2025 full-year spread was PO4 1, PO6 2, PO7 4, PO9 6, PO10 1, PO11 2, PO12 2.
trend.source: Norwegian Veterinary Institute, monthly ILA update, June 2026

trend.fact: Norway: 2021 was the recent peak with 36 cases. By end-June 2025 there were 14 confirmed outbreaks, mostly in Nordland and Troms.
Faroe Islands 2024: ISA was confirmed at Bakkafrost site A-19 Vágur, holding about 1 million fish averaging about 2.6 kg. ISA is rare in the Faroes.

new_research.fact: Norway: about 190 million ISA-containing vaccine doses were sold in 2025, similar to 2024, when nearly 200 million fish were vaccinated. Pharmaq estimates about 40% of Norwegian salmon are ISA-vaccinated. 2025 was the first time several outbreaks hit vaccinated fish at once.

Risk factors for ISA outbreaks with no known source (Norway 2004-2017): a stocking period longer than 2 months (OR 3.9), prior IPN (OR 3.2), higher latitude, and high fish density. The mean annual probability of a primary outbreak was 0.7%.
new_research.source: Lyngstad et al., Frontiers in Vet Science, 2018

new_research.fact: Norway 2019-2022: marine farms inside ISA protection or surveillance zones had about 2.2-2.3 times the odds of an outbreak.

diseases.name: Cardiomyopathy syndrome (CMS)
diseases.what: A viral heart disease ('heart rupture') that mainly kills large, fast-growing salmon late in the sea phase. Losses therefore fall on near-harvest biomass, and stress from handling or delousing can trigger sudden deaths.

mortality.fact: Norway: CMS mostly causes low to moderately elevated mortality over weeks or months, with spikes after stress such as storms, algal blooms or handling. Acute high mortality is rare.
mortality.source: Norwegian Veterinary Institute report 2017-1, CMS hos laks

mortality.fact: Norway 2025: CMS made up about 16% of infection-category death registrations, up from about 8% in 2024. It was ranked the most important disease in PO1-PO5.
mortality.source: Norwegian Veterinary Institute, Fiskehelserapporten 2025 (2026)

mortality.fact: Norway, Mar 2025: a CMS outbreak at Mowi's Rønstad site (Volda) killed 5,725 fish in four of five pens, 2,200 of them in one pen.
mortality.source: iLaks, 27 May 2025

growth.fact: CMS mainly hits large, fast-growing fish, typically in the second year at sea, so each loss is of high-weight biomass. It is now also seen as early as 5 months after sea transfer and in fish of 100-300 g.

cost.fact: Norway: direct industry losses were NOK 33.5-66.3 million per year (2003 estimate). In 2007 Marine Harvest lost 1,200 t of biomass to CMS in H1, implying more than NOK 200 million for the sector that year. No newer health-economic estimate existed as of 2017.

trend.fact: Norway: CMS was diagnosed at 114 sites in 2025, up from 78 in 2024 (129 in 2023).

new_research.fact: Benchmark Genetics (2026): genomic selection for CMS resistance raised field survival in a natural outbreak from 73.8% (mid-ranked families) to 87.5% (top families). Heritability of resistance was 0.50-0.59 in challenge tests and 0.30 for field survival. Paper: 'From Challenge Tests to Field Survival…', Aquaculture 2026.
There is still no commercial CMS vaccine. The NVI project HSMI-CMS-Vacc worked on vaccine development (page seen only in search results).

diseases.name: Heart and skeletal muscle inflammation (HSMI)
diseases.what: The most widespread viral disease of Norwegian farmed salmon. It inflames heart and red muscle, usually in the first months at sea, causing fish to lose appetite and making them vulnerable to handling stress.

mortality.fact: Norway: mortality in affected pens ranges from negligible to about 20%, with high morbidity. Heart inflammation can run for 1-2 months without visible signs.
mortality.source: Norwegian Veterinary Institute, HSMI page

mortality.fact: Norway 2025: HSMI made up about 19% of infection-category death registrations. It was ranked the most important disease in PO6-PO13.
mortality.source: Norwegian Veterinary Institute, Fiskehelserapporten 2025 (2026)

quality.fact: Up to 20% of fillets at Norwegian processing plants were reported to have melanised (dark) spots, which cause downgrading. PRV was found in all red and melanised foci studied and is proposed as a precondition for them.

Caveat: Nofima (2022) found rib fractures may be the main cause of melanin spots, rising from about 4 to 10 rib defects per fish after sea transfer. Dark spots are called the most common quality problem in farmed salmon.

trend.fact: Norway: HSMI was diagnosed at 167 sites in 2025, up from 115 in 2024 (184 in 2023).

Norway: PRV-1 is found in almost 90% of sea-phase farmed salmon, and nearly all fish are infected during the cycle. HSMI is also diagnosed in Chile, Scotland and Ireland, and to a lesser extent in western Canada.

new_research.fact: 2025: host genotype mattered more than virus genotype. Heart inflammation after PRV-1 challenge reached 62% in a European Mowi strain versus 29% in a New Brunswick strain, so genetics or breeding could lower HSMI.
Norway: the FHF-funded PRVariant project (Nov 2025-2027, led by NMBU) is mapping PRV-1 variants with different virulence. There is still no HSMI vaccine on the market.
An experimental inactivated PRV vaccine protected against HSMI after injection challenge but gave only moderate protection under natural cohabitation.

keywords: inflamación del músculo esquelético y cardíaco

diseases.name: Gill disease (complex gill disease, AGD)
diseases.agent: Multifactorial: Paramoeba (Neoparamoeba) perurans (AGD), Candidatus Branchiomonas cysticola, salmon gill poxvirus (SGPV), Desmozoon lepeophtherii, plus plankton and micro-jellyfish and warm water
diseases.what: Damaged gills reduce oxygen uptake, so fish tolerate warm water, handling and delousing poorly. Gill disease is now a leading cause of mass mortality in Norway and Scotland, and AGD needs repeated freshwater or peroxide baths.

mortality.fact: Scotland (Shetland), 2025: Scottish Sea Farms reported full-cycle mortality of 69% at East of Papa Little, and monthly mortality of 10.5-13% at Cole Deep and 19.6% at Holms Geo. The cause was AGD and gill problems after record sea temperatures, plankton and micro-jellyfish.
mortality.source: Fish Farming Expert, 10 Feb 2026

mortality.fact: Norway 2025: complex gill disease was ranked the second most important cause of salmon mortality and the fastest-growing problem. It made up about 20% of unknown-cause death registrations nationally (about 30% in PO1-PO4), up from 3-14% in 2021-2024.
mortality.source: Norwegian Veterinary Institute, Fiskehelserapporten 2025 (2026)

mortality.fact: Norway cohort study (8 sites): gill-related mortality occurred in 10 of 16 sea groups but was low per group (0.04-1.69%). Gill infections were very common: Ca. Branchiomonas in 78% of gills, D. lepeophtherii 82%, P. perurans 20%, SGPV 14%.
mortality.source: Østevik et al., J Fish Dis, 2022 (FHF PDF)

mortality.fact: Untreated AGD can kill up to about 10% per week (Tasmania). In Norway's first outbreaks in 2006, mortality was 10-20% at three farms and about 80% at one.
mortality.source: VKM risk assessment of AGD, 2014

growth.fact: AGD halved aerobic capacity compared with healthy-gilled salmon (Hvas et al. 2017, cited in FHR 2025). This limits growth and tolerance of handling.
2025-26 breeding study: a negative genetic correlation (about −0.17 to −0.21) was found between gill damage score and body weight.
growth.source: Preston et al., Frontiers in Aquaculture, 2025/2026

cost.fact: Scotland 2025: gill-driven losses turned Scottish Sea Farms to a full-year operating loss of NOK −128m (versus +NOK 555m in 2024), with Q4 EBIT/kg of NOK −33.8. 2025 harvest was 32,800 t gwt, and 2026 guidance was cut from 45,000 t to 43,000 t.
Scotland 2012: one company estimated its AGD cost at about NOK 45 million, and another lost 4,661 t of salmon in Shetland.

trend.fact: Norway 2025: detections of P. perurans (AGD) were 'far higher' than in 2024 (no count given). SGPV was detected at 191 sites, about the same as previous years. Bacterial gill disease fell to about 9% of infection registrations in PO1-PO4 (16% in 2024, 29% in 2023).

Scotland: an analysis of mass-mortality events found poor gill health was the most common general cause, in 65% of cases. About 21 million fish from the 2022 smolt year class died prematurely at sea (advocacy-group letter citing Scottish Government data).
trend.source: Coastal Communities Network letter to Scottish Parliament RAI Committee, Mar 2026

new_research.fact: Genetic resistance to complex gill disease: gill-damage score heritability was about 0.29, and genomic prediction accuracy was 0.60-0.62 (Benchmark Genetics/Stirling, 3,120 fish, 195 families). Selective breeding is feasible.
new_research.source: Preston et al., Frontiers in Aquaculture, 2025/2026

new_research.fact: AGD treatment: freshwater baths of 2-3 h work best, and hydrogen peroxide is less effective and riskier. Norway's 2022 cohort study saw mixed results, with AGD decreasing after baths in 6 groups and increasing in 5.

diseases.name: SRS (piscirickettsiosis)
diseases.what: A bacterial blood infection that is Chile's top infectious killer of farmed salmon and the reason for almost all Chilean antibiotic use; it has now also hit Tasmania and is rising in Ireland and Scotland.

mortality.fact: Chile 2025: SRS caused 52.8% of Atlantic salmon infectious mortality, up 9.6 points on 2024 (Sernapesca annual report).
mortality.source: Salmon Business on Sernapesca, 2026

mortality.fact: Chile 2023: SRS caused 44.7% of Atlantic salmon infectious mortality, down 8.1% on 2022.
mortality.source: WeAreAquaculture on Sernapesca, 2024

mortality.fact: Tasmania 2025: more than 20,000 t of farmed salmon died, mainly from P. salmonis; the February peak alone was 6,300 t. Production was about 68,000 t gutted weight in FY2024-25.
mortality.source: Fish Farming Expert on EPA Tasmania data, 2026

mortality.fact: Tasmania Jan-Mar 2026: another 9,197 t died (2,025 / 3,356 / 3,816 t by month), about 12% of annual production. The article does not confirm the cause, but P. salmonis and warm water are the suspected drivers.
mortality.source: Huon News on EPA data, Apr 2026

mortality.fact: Ireland and Scotland since 2023: Piscirickettsia found at more than 25 marine sites a year, most with clinical signs. Mean outbreak length is 13 weeks (range 4-26). Norway had at least 7 affected farms in 2024 without significant mortality.
mortality.source: Fish Farming Expert on Norwegian Veterinary Institute study, 2026

mortality.fact: Norway 2025: no confirmed SRS in salmon; suspected at 3 sites in PO8/PO9. SRS became a listed disease (category G) in June 2025.
mortality.source: Norwegian Veterinary Institute, Fish Health Report 2025

growth.fact: Chile Q1 2026: Salmones Camanchaca cited lower harvest weights after SRS outbreaks; processing cost rose 15% to US$1.22/kg WFE. No weight figure was given.

cost.fact: Chile: infectious disease costs the salmon industry more than US$700 million a year in lost revenue, with SRS the main driver.
Chile Q1 2026: SRS outbreaks at several Camanchaca sites cost US$2.8 million in extraordinary mortality. EBITDA fell 52% to US$9.3 million and EBIT/kg fell from US$1.02 to US$0.35.
Chile 2024: 336.3 t of antibiotics were used, up 9.7% year on year. That is 302 g per tonne harvested over a full cycle. Florfenicol was 97% of the total and SRS accounted for more than 96%.
Chile 2024: 351.1 t of antimicrobials were used and 97.9% of sea-phase treatments targeted SRS. About 99% were given as medicated feed.
Chile 2024: cycles certified under PROA-Salmon used 18.9 g antibiotics per tonne, more than 90% below the 302 g/t average. They covered 28.7% of harvest.

trend.fact: Chile: SRS share of Atlantic salmon infectious mortality was 44.7% in 2023, about 43% in 2024 (implied) and 52.8% in 2025, so it is rising again. Total Chilean salmonid mortality was 9.7% in 2025, down 1.5 points.
Tasmania: Australia approved emergency florfenicol use in Nov 2025, with 10-day treatments at Tassal and Huon leases (Meads Creek, Stringers Cove, Zuidpool, Soldiers Point).

Tasmania: one P. salmonis genotype is present, in the south-east since 2023 and on the east coast since at least 2021. Outbreaks follow sea transfer at 12-18°C, and eastern Tasmanian waters are warming nearly 4x faster than the global average.
trend.source: NRE Tasmania, Reflections and Learnings, Salmon Mortality Event 2025

new_research.fact: A live attenuated SRS vaccine (PHARMAQ/Zoetis) protected Atlantic salmon for at least 15 months in lab challenges. Protection failed if fish were immunised at 7-8°C (32-66% mortality) but held at 10°C or above. About 95% of Atlantic salmon stocked in Chile's regions X and XI (141 million fish) were vaccinated in 2022.
Genomics: SRS resistance is heritable (h2 about 0.27-0.39 genomic). Genomic prediction raised reliability 25-29% over pedigree selection.
Mowi Scotland has an SRS vaccine in development and is researching bacteriophage therapy as an antibiotic alternative.

damage.title: What SRS destroys in Chile, as far as public data allow
lines: About 8,000 t of salmon killed by SRS in 2025 (our estimate): 60,273 t of dead fish in all, 25.7 % of deaths from infectious causes, 52.8 % of those from SRS (Sernapesca 2025 report; the Atlantic salmon share is applied to all species).
An outbreak typically kills 20–30 % of the fish in a cage group, up to 90 %, and about 60 % of sea farms are affected at some point (Sernapesca, SRS programme resolution 2026).
Losses put at about US$700 million a year for the industry (same resolution).
More than 95 % of the antibiotics used in Chilean salmon farming go against SRS: about 340 g per tonne harvested in 2024.

What public data cannot show: deaths farm by farm and month by month (Sernapesca publishes yearly, by company and region), and the weight lost by fish harvested early, which companies mention without figures (Camanchaca Q1 2026).
damage.source: Sernapesca, Informe Sanitario 2025; Sernapesca SRS programme resolution 2026; see the study library below.

themes.name: Growth, harvest weight and early harvests

studies.title: Sernapesca 2025 health report: overall mortality falls, Tenacibaculosis rises (news summary)
studies.finding: In 2025 infectious causes were 25.7% of Atlantic salmon mortality and SRS was 52.8% of that, up from 2024 and back to being the top infectious killer; Tenacibaculosis was 31.5%. Total salmonid mortality was 9.7% (60,273 t dead biomass), down 1.5 points on 2024.

studies.title: Chile recorded only one ISA outstanding outbreak in 2023 (Sernapesca 2023 health report)
studies.finding: In 2023 SRS caused 44.7% of infectious mortality in Atlantic salmon (Tenacibaculosis 37.9%), down from 2022. Average closed-cycle mortality was 9.4% for Atlantic salmon.

studies.title: Chilean salmonid production hampered by increased mortality (Sernapesca H1 2024)
studies.finding: In H1 2024 SRS was 42% of infectious mortality in Atlantic salmon and 52% in rainbow trout. Accumulated mortality in Atlantic salmon closed groups rose to 11.4% from 10.3% in H1 2023; 15.3 million salmonids died at sea in six months.

studies.title: Why Does Piscirickettsia salmonis Break the Immunological Paradigm in Farmed Salmon? Biological Context to Understand the Relative Control of Piscirickettsiosis
studies.finding: In 2020 SRS caused 47.8% of infectious mortality in Atlantic salmon (67.3% in trout), i.e. 11.7% of all Atlantic salmon deaths. Losses are put at about US$700 million a year, and a median 93.5% of antibiotic volume in 2017-2020 went to SRS.

studies.title: Resolución Exenta DN-00980/2026: new Programa Sanitario Específico de Vigilancia y Control de Piscirickettsiosis
studies.finding: The regulator's 2026 SRS programme says outbreaks in Los Lagos and Aysén can kill 20-30% of a stock and in some cases up to 90%, with about 60% of marine sites reporting the disease and losses of about US$700 million a year. It replaces the 2012-2013 programme.

studies.title: Use of regulatory data to describe and identify risk factors for salmonid rickettsial septicaemia in Chile, 2011-2017
studies.finding: Analysis of Sernapesca databases 2011-2017: the farmed species was the key driver of both whether a cycle had SRS mortality and how high it was; trout cycles were much less likely than Atlantic salmon to report SRS mortality (incidence risk ratio 0.17).

studies.title: Epidemiology of piscirickettsiosis on selected Atlantic salmon (Salmo salar) and rainbow trout (Oncorhynchus mykiss) salt water aquaculture farms in Chile
studies.finding: On 14 Atlantic salmon farms (252 cages, 2010-2012) SRS hit a high share of cages; onset came at about 2,480-3,829 degree-days after sea transfer depending on vaccine. No vaccine prevented SRS, and high mortality in the first 4 weeks at sea predicted earlier outbreaks.

studies.title: Co-Infection by LF-89-Like and EM-90-Like Genogroups of Piscirickettsia salmonis in Farmed Atlantic Salmon in Chile
studies.finding: SRS caused 10.2% of total Atlantic salmon mortality in H1 2022. In 6 prospective farms the bacterium was first detected 83-197 days after sea entry, and both genogroups often co-infect farms, while the only live vaccine contains just one (EM-90).

studies.title: SRS: A disease that eats away the Chilean salmon
studies.finding: An early industry estimate put SRS losses at about US$100 million a year (likely higher by 2015), with about US$800,000 of antibiotic spending per percentage point of SRS mortality. SRS was then 60-70% of infectious losses in Atlantic and coho salmon, and used ~82% of 338 t of antibiotics.

studies.title: Salmones Camanchaca: SRS outbreaks and weak prices cut Q1 EBITDA by 52%
studies.finding: SRS outbreaks at several sites cost Camanchaca US$2.8 million in extraordinary mortality in Q1 2026; EBIT per kg fell from US$1.02 to US$0.35 (SRS plus lower prices) and EBITDA fell 52% to US$9.3m. Lower harvest weights pushed processing cost up 15% to US$1.22/kg.

studies.title: Salmones Camanchaca's profit plummeted in Q1 2026
studies.finding: SRS outbreaks at two sites forced Camanchaca to bring harvests forward, giving lower-than-planned fish weights; the event is a concrete case of SRS turning into early harvest of small fish (no volume or kg given).

studies.title: Lower mortality and higher productivity for Chilean salmon industry last year (Aquabench 2023)
studies.finding: Atlantic salmon closed-cycle mortality fell to 9.7% in 2023 from 13.4% in 2022, and yield rose 4% to 4.53 kg harvested per smolt; average Atlantic harvest weight was 5.1 kg. SRS was cited as one of the biggest killers (33%, base unclear).

studies.title: Novel insights into the genetic relationship between growth and disease resistance in an aquaculture strain of Coho salmon
studies.finding: In an SRS challenge (coho), daily growth fell from 1.11 g/day before infection to about 0.69 g/day during it, and survivors grew 2.09 g/day faster than fish that died. Faster early growth was genetically linked to longer survival (r=0.43), but survival time and harvest weight were unfavourably correlated (-0.50).

studies.title: Chile fish health and growth best in five years (INTESAL)
studies.finding: Between 2013 and 2018 Chilean mortality fell from 16% to 9%, harvest weight rose from 4.2 to 5.2 kg and the sea cycle shortened from 18 to 16.5 months, while antibiotic use fell to 322.7 t; this is baseline context for how disease control lifts harvest weight.

studies.title: Study: antibiotic injection is better than in-feed treatment for SRS (Aquabench)
studies.source: Fish Farming Expert (seminar presentation, not peer reviewed)
studies.finding: Aquabench data on more than 10 billion fish (2017-2024): injecting oxytetracycline instead of medicated feed roughly halved SRS mortality, cut total antibiotic use by 26% and raised harvest weight by 23%. Industry benchmarking, not a peer-reviewed study.

studies.title: Current Status of the Use of Antibiotics and the Antimicrobial Resistance in the Chilean Salmon Farms
studies.finding: Gives Sernapesca antibiotic use 2005-2016: from 143 t (2010) to a peak of 563 t (2014) and 557 t (630 g/t) in 2015, then 382.5 t in 2016. In 2016 florfenicol was 82.5% of use, 95% was at sea mainly against P. salmonis, and SRS caused 74.6% of Atlantic salmon infectious mortality.

studies.title: Health Situation of Chilean Salmon Industry
studies.source: Sernapesca presentation hosted by Norwegian Veterinary Institute
studies.finding: Official Sernapesca table 2007-2018: use 393.9 t (497 g/t) in 2017 and 322.7 t (380 g/t) in 2018, an 18% drop in tonnes and 24% in g/t. Mortality from P. salmonis was falling in H1 2019 while Tenacibaculum and AGD rose.

studies.title: SRS pushed Chilean salmon farming antibiotic use up by 9.7% last year
studies.finding: Antibiotic use rose 9.7% in 2024 to 336.26 t (301 production cycles), with SRS behind more than 96% and florfenicol 96.98% of use. Consumption index 0.034% (about 340 g/t) vs 0.031% in 2023; closed-cycle index 302.33 g/t. PROA-certified farms used 93.7% less.

studies.title: Insights and Lessons from Chilean Salmon Aquaculture on Antimicrobial Use
studies.finding: Review: Sernapesca reports 351.1 t of antimicrobials used in 2024, 97.9% of treatments given in the sea grow-out phase against SRS. (Note the 336 t figure elsewhere appears to cover a narrower base.)

studies.title: Antimicrobial use in Chile's salmon farming industry dropped 32 percent in 2022
studies.finding: Antibiotic use fell from 463.4 t (470 g/t) in 2021 to 341.5 t (320 g/t) in 2022, the lowest rate since reporting began in 2007; 97.7% of use was in the sea phase.

studies.title: Salmoneras explican las razones del fuerte aumento en el uso de antibioticos reportado por Sernapesca
studies.finding: The 2021 rate jumped 34% to 470 g/t (vs 630 g/t in 2015 and 340-350 g/t in 2018-2020). The Consejo del Salmon (AquaChile, Australis, Cermaq, Mowi, Salmones Aysen) said SRS causes more than 95% of Chilean antibiotic use.

studies.title: Resolución Exenta DN-01151/2026 modifying the antimicrobial use programme (Res. 8228/2015)
studies.finding: Sets antibiotic-use bands that reward low users: Atlantic salmon farms with 0 g/t, up to 250 g/t, or 250-400 g/t get 10%, 7% or 3% exceptions on allowed losses; 400 g/t equals the 2022-2025 Atlantic salmon average. SRS mortality at sea has trended up since 2018 (+42% from 2019 to 2020).

studies.title: A Novel and Validated Protocol for Performing MIC Tests to Determine the Susceptibility of Piscirickettsia salmonis Isolates to Florfenicol and Oxytetracycline
studies.finding: Of 58 Chilean field isolates, 56% were non-wild-type (reduced susceptibility) to florfenicol and 9% to oxytetracycline. This is an early warning for the drug that now makes up ~97% of use.

studies.title: Chile: freshwater salmon antibiotic use drops 34% in 2025
studies.finding: Freshwater antibiotic use fell 34.1% in 2025, but the national consumption index (dominated by sea-phase SRS treatment) rose 5.88%, a second year of increase.

studies.title: Chilean farmers cut antibiotic use in 2019
studies.finding: Use fell 6% to 303.2 t in 2019 with harvests up 13% to 953,395 t; the consumption index fell from 0.038% to 0.032% (about 380 to 320 g/t). Chile's higher use than Norway/Scotland is blamed on SRS being hard to vaccinate against.

studies.title: Why vaccines fail against Piscirickettsiosis in farmed salmon and trout and how to avoid it: A review
studies.finding: About 46 million salmonids died of SRS in 2012-2020; SRS fell from 84.3% to 43.3% of infectious deaths (all species) over the period. Of 28 registered vaccines only 3 claim to cut mortality; in field data (Happold et al. 2020) the best Atlantic salmon regimen cut SRS mortality only 22% and others were worse. Losses are over US$700m/yr.

studies.title: Commercial Vaccines Do Not Confer Protection against Two Genogroups of Piscirickettsia salmonis, LF-89 and EM-90, in Atlantic Salmon
studies.finding: In controlled challenges, a commercial vaccine gave negative relative survival (RPS -9% vs LF-89, -12% vs EM-90), with survival 56.7% vs 60.3% and 60.2% vs 64.6% for vaccinated vs unvaccinated; the regulator's threshold is 70% RPS. About 43% of farmers use the pentavalent vaccine.

studies.title: The Effect of an Attenuated Live Vaccine against Salmonid Rickettsial Septicemia in Atlantic Salmon Is Highly Dependent on Water Temperature during Immunization
studies.finding: The live vaccine ALPHA JECT LiVac SRS (licensed in Chile 2016) protected for at least 15 months in lab tests when fish were vaccinated at 10 C or above, but lost much of its protection at 7-8 C. Holding fish at 15 C for 5 days after vaccination restored it, so cold freshwater vaccination is one reason for field failure.

studies.title: Increased survival and reduced bacterial shedding following single but not repeated oral immunizations against Piscirickettsia salmonis in Atlantic salmon
studies.source: Bulletin of the European Association of Fish Pathologists 44(3)
studies.finding: Canadian lab trial: one oral dose gave modest protection (RPS 30.9%) and less shedding; four doses gave RPS 21.1% and two doses none. The authors blame partly the mismatch between the Chilean vaccine strain and the Canadian isolate.

studies.title: Genomic predictions can accelerate selection for resistance against Piscirickettsia salmonis in Atlantic salmon
studies.finding: Using a 50K SNP chip raised the accuracy of breeding values for SRS resistance by 8-25% (days to death) and 27-30% (survival) over pedigree-only selection, and about 20K SNPs was enough. This supports genomic selection as a practical route to more resistant stock.

studies.title: GWAS meta-analysis of resistance against Piscirickettsia salmonis in Atlantic salmon
studies.finding: On 5,858 challenged fish from 3 breeding lines, SNP heritability of SRS survival was 0.12-0.33 (time to death 0.19-0.44). No single large-effect gene was found (top SNP explains 0.5-1.3%), so gains must come from genomic selection on many genes, not a single marker.

studies.title: Investigating mechanisms underlying genetic resistance to Salmon Rickettsial Syndrome in Atlantic salmon using RNA sequencing
studies.finding: In a challenge of 2,265 fish from 96 families (33% mortality), heritability of SRS survival was 0.43, at the top of the 0.11-0.41 range of earlier Atlantic salmon studies. The trait is highly polygenic, with no major QTL.

studies.title: Hendrix Genetics ups SRS resistance 15-20 percent
studies.finding: In a challenge test of about 1,500 fish, the top 25 fish by genomic breeding value had 80% survival vs 8.2% for the population. The company projected about 23% lower SRS mortality under Chilean farm conditions (preliminary, company data).

studies.title: Hydrodynamic connectivity, water temperature, and salinity are major drivers of piscirickettsiosis prevalence and transmission among salmonid farms in Chile
studies.finding: A hydrodynamic model found that the strongest predictors of SRS were infected farms upstream and the size of their outbreaks, followed by seawater temperature and salinity. Downstream farms reached close to 100% prevalence by week 25, against about 10% for unexposed farms by week 56.

studies.title: Is between-farm water-borne pathogen dissemination an important driver in the epidemiology of salmonid rickettsial septicaemia in Chile?
studies.finding: Using 334 Los Lagos farms and 1,010 cycles (2012-2018), the study found only a weak link between SRS mortality on a farm and its neighbours, concluding water-borne spread is not the main driver. This contrasts with Bravo et al. 2020.

studies.title: Eliciting expert judgements to estimate risk and protective factors for Piscirickettsiosis in Chilean salmon farming
studies.finding: Experts ranked net fouling, dense neighbouring farms, sea lions and early-maturing fish as risk factors for severe outbreaks. Synchronised fallowing, timely diagnosis and necropsy training were ranked protective.

studies.title: How problem child El Nino threatens Chilean fish farming
studies.finding: Reports a new Chilean paper listing El Nino effects as more algal blooms, hypoxia, SRS and lice. It recalls 2016, when a warm-water bloom killed more than 100,000 t at about 37 sites (losses over US$800m). No direct El Nino-SRS numbers are given.

studies.title: Chilean salmon sector prepares for El Nino-related disruptions
studies.finding: Industry sources warn that El Nino means warm, stratified water, slower growth, worse FCR and longer cycles even before any mass mortality; the 2016 El Nino bloom killed about 27 million fish in Los Lagos. SRS is not quantified.

studies.title: Caligus rogercresseyi infestation is associated with Piscirickettsia salmonis-attributed mortalities in farmed salmonids in Chile
studies.finding: Field data: higher adult Caligus abundance in the 10 weeks before an SRS outbreak (weekly SRS mortality over 0.1%) predicted significantly higher cumulative SRS mortality in the next 10 weeks, in both Atlantic salmon and trout. The authors call lice control part of SRS control.

studies.title: Disease Resistance in Atlantic Salmon (Salmo salar): Coinfection of the Intracellular Bacterial Pathogen Piscirickettsia salmonis and the Sea Louse Caligus rogercresseyi
studies.finding: In a challenge of 1,634 fish, SRS alone killed 251 of 545 (46%), while SRS plus lice killed all 1,089 coinfected fish. Resistance stayed heritable (h2 0.17-0.24), but the genetic correlation between single-infection and coinfection resistance was weak, so breeding for one does not guarantee the other.

studies.title: Epidemiology of Salmonid Rickettsial Septicemia (SRS) in Farmed Salmon: The Role of Sea Lice Infestations in Mortality Risk
studies.finding: Farm data 2014-2021: weekly SRS mortality peaks in warmer seasons; egg-bearing female lice levels predicted both higher weekly SRS mortality and an earlier first outbreak. Lice rose over the period while SRS risk stayed flat.

studies.title: Skretting functional diet 'best against SRS in trial' (GSI benchmark of functional feeds)
studies.finding: A GSI-coordinated 2018 cohabitation trial compared 4 commercial functional diets; the company reported a 78% lower probability of SRS death than controls for the best diet. Only company-reported numbers were published.

studies.title: Know Your Enemy: Piscirickettsia salmonis and Phage Interactions Using an In Silico Perspective
studies.finding: Of 79 P. salmonis genomes, about 70% carry prophages and many have anti-phage defence systems. This is groundwork for phage therapy, which is computational only and not yet tested in fish, so it is years from farms.

studies.title: Data shows salmon mortality event unprecedented
studies.finding: Over 5,500 t of salmon mortality waste was received in February 2025 alone, with hundreds of pen notifications in the D'Entrecasteaux Channel. The Chief Veterinary Officer attributed the event largely to endemic P. salmonis in warm summer water.

studies.title: Reflections and Learnings: Salmon Mortality Event 2025
studies.finding: The official review confirms the Tasmanian strain is P. salmonis, a single genotype present on the east coast since at least 2021 and in the south-east since 2023. The Jan-Apr 2025 event, peaking in February, hit Huon and Tassal; an emergency florfenicol permit was sought.

studies.title: More than 20,000 tonnes of fish died prematurely in Tasmania last year
studies.finding: Tasmanian salmon mortality exceeded 20,000 t in 2025 (6,300 t in February), against production of about 68,000 t gutted weight in 2024-25, a loss on the order of a quarter of output. Florfenicol feed had been used 13 times since November 2025.

studies.title: Dead salmon: 9,000 tonnes in 12 weeks
studies.finding: In January-March 2026, 9,197 t of salmon died on Tasmanian farms (2,025 / 3,356 / 3,816 t by month), about 12% of annual production. This shows the P. salmonis problem recurred in the second summer.

studies.title: Salmon piscirickettsiosis in Europe: a disease of increasing concern
studies.source: Bulletin of the European Association of Fish Pathologists 45(3)
studies.finding: Ireland and Scotland went from 0-10 clinical cases a year before 2019 to over 30 farm cases a year since. Mortality averages 1-2% of stock per week and can exceed 25% cumulatively if untreated; SRS now drives most antibiotic prescriptions there, and a new species (P. nova) is involved.

studies.title: Piscirickettsiosis (SRS) in the North-East Atlantic area (PisciNor project)
studies.authors: Rodger H, Olsen AB, Colquhoun DJ et al.
studies.source: Fish Farming Expert (Norwegian Veterinary Institute / PatoGen / Marine Institute)
studies.finding: Since 2023 Piscirickettsia has been detected each year at more than 25 marine sites across Ireland and Scotland, most with clinical disease; outbreaks last a mean of 13 weeks at about 13.9 C. Norway had at least 7 affected farms in 2024 without significant mortality and made SRS notifiable again in June 2025.

studies.title: Fish Health Report 2025 (Norway)
studies.finding: Piscirickettsiosis was listed as a notifiable disease in Norway from 15 June 2025. In 2025 there was one confirmed case, in turbot, and three salmon suspicions that were not confirmed, so there is no supply impact in Norway yet.

studies.title: New SRS bacteria species discovered in Scotland and Ireland (Piscirickettsia nova)
studies.finding: PatoGen researchers identified a distinct species, provisionally P. nova, causing SRS-like disease in Irish and Scottish salmon. Over half of Scottish 2021-2024 'P. salmonis' PCR positives re-tested were P. nova (per Rodger et al. 2025), so Chilean vaccines may not transfer.

studies.title: Cullen Scholarship: Epidemiological examination of SRS in Irish Atlantic salmon farms
studies.finding: SRS accounted for 80% of antibiotics used in Irish salmon farming in 2022, and the disease has been increasing in recent years. (Year of the document inferred, not stated.)

studies.title: Advice from the assessment of the risk to Fraser River Sockeye Salmon due to Piscirickettsia salmonis transfer from Atlantic Salmon farms in the Discovery Islands area, British Columbia
studies.finding: BC Atlantic salmon farms recorded 36 farm-level SRS diagnoses in 2002-2016 (9 of 15 years), a low-level endemic problem with nothing like Chilean losses. DFO judged the risk to wild sockeye minimal.

studies.title: Hindcasting Farmed Salmon Mortality to Improve Future Health and Production Outcomes
studies.finding: New Zealand king salmon (not Atlantic): a rickettsia-like organism modelled on P. salmonis contributed to a 2021/22 event that lost about 1,300 t, roughly 10% of national output. Mortality switched on above about 17 C, showing how warming turns a background infection into a supply event.

srs_share_of_infectious_mortality_atlant.unit: % of infectious-cause mortality, Atlantic salmon, sea phase
srs_share_of_infectious_mortality_atlant.source: Sernapesca annual health reports, as cited by Miranda et al. 2018 (2016), Rozas-Serri 2022 (2020), WeAreAquaculture (2023), Salmon Business (2025)
srs_share_of_infectious_mortality_atlant.note: 2016 value is quoted by Miranda et al. as SRS share of Atlantic salmon mortality (assumed infectious-cause basis, as in Sernapesca reports). H1 2024 = 42% (half-year only, Fish Farming Expert). 2022 and 2024 full-year values were only given as relative changes (-8.1% / +9.6%) and are left out. Years 2012-2015, 2017-2019, 2021 not found.

srs_share_of_infectious_mortality_all_sa.source: Valenzuela-Aviles et al. 2022, Table 1 (Sernapesca data, salmon and trout combined)
srs_share_of_infectious_mortality_all_sa.note: Only endpoints extracted; 2012-2020 total 71.0%; ~46 million fish died of SRS 2012-2020.

antibiotics_tonnes_chile.unit: tonnes active ingredient, all salmonid farming (fresh + sea)
antibiotics_tonnes_chile.source: Sernapesca, via Miranda et al. 2018 (2005-2016), Sernapesca/Sandoval 2019 (2017-2018), Fish Farming Expert (2019), SeafoodSource (2021-2022), Farias et al. 2025 (2024)
antibiotics_tonnes_chile.note: 2020, 2023 and 2025 totals not found. 2024: Fish Farming Expert reports 336.26 t (narrower base, 301 cycles); Farias et al. say 351.1 t. Valenzuela-Aviles 2022 gives 413.5 t for 2021, conflicting with Sernapesca's 463.4 t.

antibiotics_g_per_t.unit: g active ingredient per tonne harvested (Sernapesca ICA x 10,000)
antibiotics_g_per_t.source: Miranda et al. 2018 (2005-2016); Sernapesca/Sandoval 2019 (2017-2018); Fish Farming Expert (2019, ICA 0.032%); SeafoodSource (2020 ICA 0.035%, 2021-2022); Fish Farming Expert (2023 ICA 0.031%, 2024 ICA 0.034%)
antibiotics_g_per_t.note: Sources disagree for 2019-2020: El Mostrador reports 298 g/t for 2020; Diario Financiero says 340-350 g/t for 2018-2020. 2024 closed-cycle index = 302.33 g/t. 2025: national ICA +5.88% vs 2024 (value not given).

atlantic_salmon_closed_cycle_mortality_c.note: All causes. Sernapesca gives 9.4% for 2023 closed cycles.

tasmania_salmon_mortality_tonnes.source: EPA Tasmania data via Fish Farming Expert and Huon News
tasmania_salmon_mortality_tonnes.note: All-cause mortality; P. salmonis the main driver per Tasmanian CVO. 2025 is 'more than 20,000 t' (FFE) / 20,133 t (Huon News).

library.note: Library compiled on 8–9 Nov 2026 from free-to-read sources; each entry was read (abstract only when the paper is paywalled). Updated by hand; the automatic publication feed below adds new papers every morning.

diseases.name: Bacterial kidney disease (BKD)
diseases.agent: Renibacterium salmoninarum (Gram-positive bacterium, passed vertically through eggs)
diseases.what: A slow, chronic bacterial infection of the kidney with no effective vaccine or cure; it is mainly a coho problem in Chile and an occasional but worrying outbreak in Norway.

mortality.fact: BKD can cause up to 40% cumulative mortality in farmed Atlantic salmon (review statement; reported in Canada and Chile).
mortality.source: Eslamloo et al., Frontiers in Immunology, 2020

mortality.fact: Chile 2023: BKD was the main infectious cause of death in coho salmon (no % given).
mortality.source: WeAreAquaculture on Sernapesca, 2024

mortality.fact: In a challenge trial, only about 21% of Atlantic salmon pre-smolts survived R. salmoninarum infection (11°C and 15°C). Family survival ranged 0-76% (unpublished data cited). Genome data show several introductions into Chile over 30 years.
mortality.source: Rozas-Serri et al., Frontiers in Immunology, 2020

trend.fact: Norway: historically 0-3 outbreaks a year. Since Dec 2022 there were 14 confirmed sites plus 2 suspected, mostly in PO6 (Hitra/Orkland, 2 companies) and PO4.
trend.source: Norwegian Veterinary Institute BKD webinar (T. Moldal), Jan 2024

trend.fact: Norway 2024: BKD was detected at 8 sites in PO5-PO6.
trend.source: Norwegian Veterinary Institute, Fish Health Report 2024

trend.fact: Norway 2025: 1 confirmed BKD outbreak (grow-out, PO5) and 1 suspected (broodstock, PO6), so a sharp fall.
trend.source: Norwegian Veterinary Institute, Fish Health Report 2025

trend.fact: Norway: no effective treatment or vaccine exists. The food authority believes BKD spread from wild fish to a sea site, then between farms via well boats and delousing vessels.
Canada (BC): DFO publishes site-level fish health events, which can be used as a feed for BKD diagnoses. No numbers were extracted.

new_research.fact: Research focus is on disease-free broodstock and egg screening, since R. salmoninarum passes through eggs. About 50 Norwegian isolates have been whole-genome sequenced to trace spread.
Poor efficacy of vaccines and antibiotics is why BKD persists in sea cages. Breeding for resistance is under study (large family differences in survival).
new_research.source: Rozas-Serri et al., Frontiers in Immunology, 2020

diseases.name: Winter ulcers and tenacibaculosis (incl. yellow mouth / mouthrot)
diseases.agent: Moritella viscosa (winter ulcer); Tenacibaculum spp. (T. finnmarkense, T. dicentrarchi in Chile, T. maritimum = yellow mouth/mouthrot in BC and Tasmania)
diseases.what: Bacterial skin and mouth ulcers that kill fish and are the main reason Norwegian salmon is downgraded at slaughter; tenacibaculosis is now Chile's number-two infectious killer.

mortality.fact: Norway 2025: winter ulcers were found at 299 salmon sites: M. viscosa at 246 (289 in 2024, 320 in 2023), Tenacibaculum at 147 (165 in 2024), and both together at 94.
mortality.source: Norwegian Veterinary Institute, Fish Health Report 2025

mortality.fact: Norway 2025: M. viscosa caused about 14% of infectious-disease death registrations (peak about 39% in 2024), about 4% of all registrations. Unspecified-bacteria winter ulcers added about 15%. Tenacibaculum mouth/head ulcers were about 12% in PO5-PO9.
mortality.source: Norwegian Veterinary Institute, Fish Health Report 2025 (AquaCloud data)

mortality.fact: Norway: at the Feb-Mar peak, winter ulcers caused 20-30% of total losses in the 2023-2025 winters, versus under 12% in 2020-2021.
mortality.source: Salmon Business, Oct 2025

mortality.fact: Chile 2025: tenacibaculosis caused 31.5% of Atlantic salmon infectious mortality, up 2.1 points. It also rose in trout (+6.8%) and coho (+4%).
mortality.source: Salmon Business on Sernapesca, 2026

mortality.fact: Chile 2023: tenacibaculosis caused 37.9% of Atlantic salmon infectious mortality, up 9% on 2022. From Jul 2018 to Aug 2020, 52.5% of marine cycles (520 of 990) had outbreaks.
mortality.source: WeAreAquaculture on Sernapesca 2024; Pontigo et al. preprint 2024

mortality.fact: BC, Canada: mouthrot can kill up to 40% of fish in affected cages (Cermaq). Yellow-mouth mortality can reach 15% (older study cited in the 2024 review).
mortality.source: Cermaq, 2022; Wassmuth et al., Frontiers in Aquaculture, 2024

cost.fact: BC: mouthrot outbreaks cost an estimated $1.8M a year plus $3.8M a year in lost revenue for the local industry. One estimate is $1.6M a year for a single company.

Chile 2019: about 6.2 t florfenicol and 3.1 t oxytetracycline were used against tenacibaculosis, 2% and 1% of the 311 t of sea antibiotics. BC 2011: 98% of aquaculture antimicrobial prescriptions were for yellow mouth.
cost.source: Pontigo et al. preprint 2024; Wassmuth et al. 2024

quality.fact: Norway: the share of salmon graded superior at slaughter rose from 80.6% in 2024 to 86.9% in 2025. Ulcers/injuries remain the main reason for downgrading. The new Moritella vaccine and fewer jellyfish problems are credited.
quality.source: Norwegian Veterinary Institute, Fish Health Report 2025

trend.fact: Norway: M. viscosa sites fell 320 (2023) to 289 (2024) to 246 (2025), but winter ulcers still ranked 5th among salmon health problems in the 2025 survey (3rd in 2024).
Chile: tenacibaculosis share of Atlantic salmon infectious mortality was about 29% (2024, implied), then 31.5% (2025), and keeps rising in all three species.
Norway: fish stocked at higher sea temperatures had fewer winter ulcers and less tenacibaculosis. Frequent handling (about every 3 weeks) in Dec-May was linked to ulcers.
trend.source: Norwegian Veterinary Institute, Fish Health Report 2025 (survey)

new_research.fact: Norway 2025: about 430 million doses of a new winter-ulcer (M. viscosa) vaccine were dispensed, and 99.4% of vaccinated salmon got it. Vets rated it good 47%, moderate 45%, poor 8%. Some reported adhesions.
new_research.source: Norwegian Veterinary Institute, Fish Health Report 2025

new_research.fact: Chile 2026: in trials of experimental T. dicentrarchi vaccines, the best prototype cut cumulative mortality to 50% versus 73.3% in controls. One prototype gave only about 10% relative protection. No commercial vaccine exists.
new_research.source: g5noticias on Avendaño-Herrera et al., J Fish Diseases, Aug 2026

new_research.fact: No commercial vaccine protects salmon against T. maritimum (yellow mouth); a BC-isolate vaccine failed in challenge trials. Cermaq and Benchmark got NOK 4.2M (2022) for a Tenacibaculum vaccine.
new_research.source: Wassmuth et al., Frontiers in Aquaculture, 2024; Cermaq 2022

diseases.name: Harmful algal blooms and jellyfish
diseases.agent: Microalgae (Pseudochattonella verruculosa, Heterosigma akashiwo, Chrysochromulina leadbeateri) and jellyfish (incl. string jellyfish Apolemia, micro-jellyfish)
diseases.what: Sudden blooms of toxic algae or swarms of jellyfish that damage gills and skin and can kill thousands of tonnes of fish within days, forcing emergency harvests.

mortality.fact: Chile 2016: a Pseudochattonella verruculosa bloom killed about 100,000 t of salmon and trout, about 15% of annual output, and cost about US$800M in exports.
mortality.source: Mardones et al., Frontiers in Marine Science, 2019

mortality.fact: Chile Apr 2021: an algal bloom killed 5,989 t across 14 farms in Los Lagos/Aysén (Mowi, AquaChile, Yadran, Multi X, Camanchaca). Camanchaca lost 1.3 million fish (US$4.4M). Heterosigma akashiwo in Comau fjord was the agent.
mortality.source: Salmon Business, 2021; Flores-Leñero et al., Toxins 2022

mortality.fact: Chile Magallanes Oct 2026: a bloom at Multi X's Taraba 7/8 sites killed about 918-959 t (sources differ). Early harvest was allowed; Sernapesca blamed physical gill damage.
mortality.source: Fish Farming Expert / Emol, Oct 2026

mortality.fact: Norway May 2019: a Chrysochromulina leadbeateri bloom in Nordland/Troms killed about 8 million salmon, about 14,100 t of biomass.
mortality.source: Fish Farming Expert on Kontali/FHF, 2019

mortality.fact: Norway Mar 2026: a Pseudochattonella bloom pushed Q1 mortality in PA1-2 to 13.3% (3.4% in Q1 2025). Nearly 1.7 million salmon died in PA1 in March.
mortality.source: Salmon Business on Mattilsynet data, May 2026

mortality.fact: Scotland 2023-24: about 1.05 million salmon died at Mowi's Loch Seaforth sites in one cycle, linked to jellyfish damaging eyes, skin and gills.
mortality.source: Undercurrent News, Oct 2024

mortality.fact: Norway 2025: algal poisoning was about 65% of environmental-cause death registrations (under 1% in 2021-24), and 94% in PO10-13. Jellyfish were about 75% of environmental deaths in 2024 but just over 1% in 2025.
mortality.source: Norwegian Veterinary Institute, Fish Health Report 2025

growth.fact: Norway 2019: losing 14,100 t of live fish meant losing about 42,000 t of potential harvest, about 3x, because fish were killed before reaching harvest weight.

cost.fact: Norway 2019 bloom: total cost about NOK 4 billion: NOK 2.1-2.4bn lost sales plus NOK 1.6-1.7bn direct and indirect costs.
Chile 2016: about US$800 million in export losses.
cost.source: Mardones et al., Frontiers in Marine Science, 2019

cost.fact: Removing and handling dead fish costs about NOK 2.12 per kg round weight in Norway (cited estimate).
cost.source: Walde et al., Preventive Veterinary Medicine 221:106062, 2023

quality.fact: Norway 2025: fewer string-jellyfish (Apolemia) problems than in 2023-24 probably cut wounds and downgrading. Superior share was 86.9% vs 80.6%.
quality.source: Norwegian Veterinary Institute, Fish Health Report 2025

trend.fact: Chile: a preventive emergency covering all 15 coastal regions runs from 1 Nov 2026 to 30 Jun 2027 because of El Niño-linked bloom risk. AquaChile warns a major bloom could overwhelm preventive measures.
Norway: algae rose to the 7th most important health challenge in the 2025 survey (15th in 2024). In 2024, jellyfish injuries ranked 3rd.
trend.source: Norwegian Veterinary Institute, Fish Health Reports 2024 and 2025

trend.fact: Scotland: gill health (incl. plankton and micro-jellyfish) was about 65% of potential persistent mortality incidents in a 2018-2024 screening of 216 sites.
trend.source: Scottish Government letter to Rural Affairs Committee, 2026

new_research.fact: Mitigations in use: bubble curtains (early Scottish trials suggest less gill damage), feed withdrawal, deep-water upwelling/aeration, and keeping fish out of surface waters.
Lab work shows Chilean P. verruculosa toxicity depends on salinity, helping explain blooms in low-salinity fjords.
new_research.source: Mardones et al., Frontiers in Marine Science, 2019

diseases.name: Pasteurellosis (and the Tasmania 2025 mortality event)
diseases.agent: Phocoenobacter atlanticus subsp. atlanticus (formerly Pasteurella atlantica genomovar salmonicida, Norway); Pasteurella skyensis (Scotland). Tasmania: Piscirickettsia salmonis plus pilchard orthomyxovirus (POMV)
diseases.what: A bacterial infection spreading along the Norwegian coast and causing farm-level losses in Scotland, linked to handling and delousing; Tasmania's 2025-26 crisis was driven by SRS in warm water, with POMV as an older viral threat.

mortality.fact: Norway 2025: pasteurellosis at 34 salmon sites (29 in 2024), in PA1-PA5 and PA7, nearly half in PA4. It caused about 3% of infectious-disease death registrations nationally and about 5% in PO5-PO9.
mortality.source: Norwegian Veterinary Institute, Fish Health Report 2025

mortality.fact: Norway 2020-2022: about 50 pasteurellosis cases a year in south-west Norway. A new lineage (Pas-4) first seen in 2018 has spread widely. Salmon mortality is generally low to moderate.
mortality.source: Gulla et al., Frontiers in Microbiology, 2023

mortality.fact: Scotland Q4 2025: a P. skyensis outbreak at Bakkafrost's Portree (Skye) site forced early emptying in October. About half of the DKK 110M quarterly loss in Scotland came from exceptional mortality.
mortality.source: Fish Farming Expert, 2026

mortality.fact: Tasmania POMV: the worst losses were in summer 2017-18, with about 1.3 million fish dead in Macquarie Harbour. A single pen can lose up to 70%.
mortality.source: FRDC, 2019

mortality.fact: Tasmania 2025: more than 20,000 t died (P. salmonis), then 9,197 t more in Jan-Mar 2026 (see SRS card).
mortality.source: Fish Farming Expert / Huon News on EPA data

cost.fact: Bakkafrost Scotland Q4 2025: farming operating loss DKK 110M (EBIT -21.11 DKK/kg), with Pasteurella at Portree a major factor. Scotland harvest fell from 27,880 gwt (2024) to 23,185 gwt (2025).

trend.fact: Norway: pasteurellosis is moving north, with outbreaks in northern Trøndelag and single cases in Andfjorden-Senja in 2024-25.
trend.source: WeAreAquaculture on Fish Health Report 2025, Mar 2026

trend.fact: Norway: a Veterinary Institute study found significantly higher pasteurellosis risk at sites using thermal or mechanical delousing (not freshwater).
trend.source: Norwegian Veterinary Institute, Fish Health Report 2025

new_research.fact: Norway: 24 applications for single-strain autogenous Pasteurella vaccines for salmon were approved (reported in FHR 2025).
new_research.source: Norwegian Veterinary Institute, Fish Health Report 2025

new_research.fact: Scotland: Mowi's autogenous vaccine (with Ridgeway Biologicals) has reduced clinical P. skyensis and Yersinia outbreaks.
Tasmania POMV: the Certovac vaccine came from a $5M program, and industry paid $2M to vaccinate the full 2019 year-class. True field efficacy was unconfirmed at the time.
Tasmania: Tegovac Plus-EC, an 8-bacteria vaccine including P. salmonis, is being considered (0.1 mL injection 6-8 weeks before sea transfer). A florfenicol risk assessment is planned.

diseases.name: Non-infectious losses: handling/treatment injury, low oxygen, high temperature, smolt quality
diseases.agent: Non-infectious: delousing and handling trauma, hypoxia, marine heatwaves, poor smoltification / low-temperature stocking
diseases.what: Deaths from fish being handled and deloused, from low oxygen or hot water, and from weak smolts put to sea, which together now kill more Norwegian salmon than infections do.

mortality.fact: Norway 2025: of sea-phase death registrations, injuries were 33.5%, infectious disease 28.1%, unknown 27.4%, physiological 4.7% and environmental 4.3% (8.5% in 2024). Data cover 408 sites, about 49% of marine sites.
mortality.source: Norwegian Veterinary Institute, Fish Health Report 2025 (AquaCloud)

mortality.fact: Norway 2025: unspecified handling injury was 13% of all registrations and non-medicinal (delousing) treatment 11%. In PO5-PO9, injuries were about 42% of deaths.
mortality.source: Norwegian Veterinary Institute, Fish Health Report 2025

mortality.fact: Norway: sea-phase mortality was 16.7% (2023, a record), 15.4% (2024) and 14.2% (2025), or 62.8M, 57.8M and 54.9M fish. A further 43.3M smolts over 3 g died in freshwater in 2025.
mortality.source: Salmon Business on Fish Health Report 2025

mortality.fact: Norway 2025: the food authority fined farmers for stocking smolts below 4°C; one cage lost 26% of fish in the first month.
mortality.source: Norwegian Veterinary Institute, Fish Health Report 2025

mortality.fact: Smolt quality: in a Norwegian trial, smolts reared on constant light had 8.8% mortality in their first 2 months at sea, versus 0.7-1.0% on short-day light regimes.
mortality.source: Gjerde et al., Frontiers in Animal Science, 2025

mortality.fact: Chile H1 2024: of 15.3M fish dead at sea (10.7M Atlantic salmon), causes were infectious 23%, mechanical damage 22%, culling 17% and environmental 16%.
mortality.source: WeAreAquaculture on Sernapesca, 2024

mortality.fact: Chile Jan 2022: low oxygen killed 2,666 t at 6 farms in Aysén (Blumar, Salmones Austral, AquaChile, Mowi); not algae-related. Jan 2024: low oxygen and algae caused a mortality peak in Los Lagos/Aysén.
mortality.source: Salmon Business 2022; Aquafeed on Sernapesca 2025

growth.fact: Norway: each delousing treatment costs an estimated EUR 0.14-0.30/kg in lost growth, on top of about NOK 0.17/kg in mortality cost.
growth.source: Walde et al., Preventive Veterinary Medicine, 2023

cost.fact: Norway: delousing treatment cost per kg live weight is thermal NOK 0.37, mechanical 0.26, freshwater 1.33 and hydrogen peroxide 0.50 (2017 estimates). Disposal of dead fish is NOK 2.12/kg.
cost.source: Walde et al., Preventive Veterinary Medicine, 2023

cost.fact: Scotland Q3 2026: Mowi's incident-based mortality cost was EUR 4.2M (EUR 2.9M a year earlier), blamed on seasonally high sea temperatures. Mowi harvested early in H1 to cut biomass at risk.

quality.fact: Norway: superior-grade share was 80.6% in 2024 and 86.9% in 2025; wounds of any cause are probably the biggest single health problem for farmed salmon.
quality.source: Norwegian Veterinary Institute, Fish Health Reports 2024/2025

trend.fact: Norway 2025: 3,918 lice-treatment weeks (+about 700), with a record level of non-medicinal treatments. 81% of fish-health staff reported a growing need for treatment, which keeps handling mortality high.
Norway 2025: 27% of salmon deaths had no known cause, a data gap.
Norway Q1 2026: national sea mortality was 3.4% (3.3% in Q1 2025), or about 12.9M fish lost.

Norway: farmers linked higher mortality to handling fish at high water temperatures with low oxygen. Routine use of the hottest thermal-delousing range (33-34°C) fell from 41% to 33% of respondents in 2025.
trend.source: Norwegian Veterinary Institute, Fish Health Report 2025

new_research.fact: Smolt production: short-day light regimes (8-12 h light) produced far more robust smolts than constant light. Smolt traits are heritable (silveriness h2 0.61), so they can be bred for.
new_research.source: Gjerde et al., Frontiers in Animal Science, 2025

new_research.fact: Mowi Scotland's post-smolt strategy (larger fish, shorter time at sea) and less handling contributed to 35% lower biomass mortality in 2024 versus 2023.

norway.title: Norway: farms (sites) with each disease diagnosed in the year
norway.source: Norwegian Veterinary Institute, Fish Health Report 2025 (Fiskehelserapporten, 2026)
norway.note: Sites where the disease was diagnosed during the year (PD: new cases). Blank: not given in the sources we read.

chile.title: Chile: share of Atlantic salmon infectious mortality by cause
chile.source: Sernapesca, health reports, via Salmon Business and WeAreAquaculture (2026)
chile.note: Share of the deaths attributed to infectious disease in Atlantic salmon. Total Chilean salmonid mortality: 9.7 % in 2025, down 1.5 points.
